before.value: The system should block the action until the required second approval or documented exception is recorded, unless an agreed emergency setting applies; users should still be able to save the request as pending and notify the approver right away, then retry after approval without re-entering everything as long as the content and target account have not changed. If the content or target account changes before approval, the pending request should be invalidated rather than silently updated, because the approval was based on a specific version. The user should resubmit so the approver is reviewing the current state, and the system should show what changed and why the old request no longer applies. Minor non-material changes, like a typo fix, may be handled as a fresh review rule, but the preference is to be conservative. A request should be invalidated if a later change affects what was approved in a meaningful way, including the text, media, destination account, audience targeting, schedule, or any compliance-sensitive setting. Minor non-substantive edits that do not change the message or destination can continue without a fresh review, but when in doubt the preference is to require a new review, especially for regulated or high-risk accounts. Material fields are the ones that can change the meaning, reach, timing, or compliance risk of the post, such as text content, images or video, target account, audience, schedule, and campaign assignment. Cosmetic fields are spelling fixes, formatting, or other edits that don’t alter the message or destination. In a middle case where a request is limited to one business unit but touches a sensitive content class or expands approval rights, it should still go to central review; local teams can make the business case and recommend it, but central should make the final call. Central may approve it as a temporary exception with an expiration and audit record.

before.value: One person drafts the content or response, another person reviews it, and someone with publishing rights sends it out; for campaigns, a contributor prepares the materials, an approver checks brand and compliance, and a publisher schedules or posts it; customer responses follow the same handoff so a message can be assigned, reviewed if needed, and answered without losing track of who did what. If content is rejected or flagged for a policy issue, it must not go out as-is; the team should be able to see exactly why it was blocked; the contributor and approver must be notified; a manager should be able to review it if there’s any question or an exception is possible; the item should stay in draft or needs revision status until it is fixed and sent back through approval. If publishing succeeds but a related piece like replies or ingestion fails, keep the core campaign running and mark the affected part as degraded rather than stopping everything; retry automatically for transient issues; escalate immediately if the failure persists, affects multiple accounts, or blocks a role needed for approval or publishing. An approval override is allowed without escalation only when the person has explicit authority for that account or campaign type, such as a designated publisher or manager acting within assigned limits. If the override goes beyond their authority, it requires a second approval from someone higher up or a documented exception process with a clear reason and timestamp, and the system should block the action until that extra approval is recorded unless an agreed emergency setting applies. When letting someone deviate from the standard campaign path, the system should also check whether the required approvals are missing, and if the deviation would bypass a required review it should block or require very explicit confirmation.

Account-specific content should be limited to people assigned to that account unless there is a formal override. A contributor might be able to draft more broadly, but approval and publishing require much tighter control and usually both the right role and direct assignment. If someone isn’t assigned, they may only view a limited version or request access, but they should not be able to publish just because their title fits.

before.value: A contributor prepares the materials, an approver checks brand and compliance, and then a publisher with publishing rights schedules or posts it; publishing stays limited to specific authorized users for control over what goes live and when. Approval can be required only when the team chooses it or when a sensitive network or campaign is involved. If an approval is missing, publishing must stop until the right person reviews it, unless an approved exception process is already in place. Mashbot should allow deviation from the standard path with clear guidance and warnings about what is being bypassed. When deviating, it should check whether the user has the right role to make the change, whether the campaign is already past a point where the change would affect published content, and whether any required approvals are missing; if the deviation could break a platform rule, cause a post to fail, or bypass a required review, it should block or require very explicit confirmation, while workflow shortcuts that do not affect compliance or publishing safety can proceed with a warning.
